Introduction

Introduction

ForewordJSW Vision and FoundationRole and Importance of Human Resources
i.

Foreword

It gives me great pleasure to introduce the JSW Motors HR Operations Manual.

As a young brand, we have a unique opportunity to build the right culture, standards and ways of working from the very beginning. The choices we make today will shape the experience of our employees, dealer partners and customers for years to come.

At JSW Motors, we believe that great customer experiences are created by engaged, capable and confident people. When our employees feel supported, developed and valued, they bring that same commitment to every customer interaction.

This manual provides a strong framework for managing the employee lifecycle, from hiring and onboarding to development, performance, rewards and separation. It is designed to help our dealer partners build consistent people practices while ensuring a positive employee experience across the network.

This guide serves as a recommended standard, not a mandate. Our dealer partners remain the employer of record and retain full responsibility for employment decisions and legal compliance. Where stronger practices already exist, we encourage partners to continue and build upon them.

As we grow together, our success will be defined not only by the vehicles we sell, but by the trust we earn from our employees, partners and customers. We look forward to building a world-class dealer network founded on strong people practices and shared success.

Together, let's create a workplace and a customer experience that sets new standards for the industry.

[Name]
[Designation], JSW Motors

iii.

Role and Importance of Human Resources

Every dealership tracks its stock, its enquiry funnel and its working capital closely, and reviews them weekly. Manpower rarely gets the same attention, even though it is usually the second or third largest line of cost after inventory. Also, India’s employment law has been rewritten and came into force in November 2025. Because labour is a concurrent subject, the HR must be aware of it.

Why this matters in our ecosystem

Three things make a dealership unusually sensitive to how its people are managed.

First, the product sells through a person. A customer buying a car will spend several hours with one consultant across two or three visits, and will make a decision that they cannot easily reverse. Their confidence in that individual is a large part of the decision. This is not a transaction that survives an indifferent or poorly informed salesperson.

Second, attrition costs far more than it appears to. When a sales consultant with three months of tenure leaves, the dealership loses the recruitment effort, the training investment, the productive time of whoever was mentoring them, and the live enquiries they were carrying. It then pays the same costs again for the replacement, who takes a further two to three months to become productive. A dealership that turns over half its front-line sales team in a year is effectively running with a permanently inexperienced floor, no matter how many people are on the roll.

Third, the relationship outlives the sale. A customer bought from a person, and expects that person to still be there when they come in for their first service or to refer a friend. Every unmanaged exit orphans a set of customers. The ones who feel orphaned are the ones who do not come back.

Culture will drive our operations on ground

"Progress is built on courage, collaboration, and commitment."

Culture is not a poster in the corridor. It is what a new joiner works out in their first fortnight by watching how people behave. In a dealership it is visible in small things: whether the morning meeting is a review or a public dressing-down, whether a consultant who reports a mistake is thanked or shouted at, whether walk-ins are allocated by a rule transparently or by favour.

We would ask dealer partners to aim for a workplace where the following are true.

  • Targets are demanding, and the means of achieving them are not negotiable. Nobody is rewarded for a number reached by cutting a corner with a customer.
  • Problems surface early, because the person who reports one is not punished for it.
  • Enquiries, walk-ins and demonstration vehicles are allocated by a published rule.
  • Managers coach on the floor rather than reviewing from a cabin.
  • Recognition is prompt and specific. Criticism is private.
  • Weekly offs and sanctioned leave are honoured. Long hours are not treated as a substitute for commitment.
  • Nobody is spoken to in an uncomfortable way.

Where these hold, the processes in this manual will work. Where they do not, no process will compensate, and the dealership will spend its time recruiting replacements for people who left for reasons no one wrote down.

If these five are being done, the dealership has a functioning HR practice.

WhatWhat it means in practice
The right people, quicklyVacancies filled within a defined turnaround time, from sources that produce candidates who last, using a consistent selection process rather than whoever walks in first.
Ready to work earlyA joiner who has an appointment letter before day one, a desk and a system login on day one, and a structured induction that gets them productive in weeks rather than months.
Clear on what is expectedEvery employee holding a written set of KPIs they have discussed with their manager, reviewed formally at least twice a year, with no surprises at appraisal time.
Paid fairly and on timeSalary on a fixed date every month without exception, incentives calculated on a published scheme and paid within a defined window, and statutory dues deposited on time.
HeardA route for raising a problem that people trust, engagement that is more than a birthday cake, and an exit process that finds out honestly why somebody left.

Position Overview

The Business Head / CEO owns the dealership's overall P&L and strategic direction, leading sales, aftersales, and value-added business functions to deliver profitable growth, brand governance, and long-term stakeholder value in a vehicle retail environment. This position is at DP level.

1. Education

Graduate / MBA in Business Administration, Management, Engineering or related field.Additional certification in Automotive Retail Management or General Management preferred.

2. Experience

18–25 years of experience in automotive dealership operations or OEM-affiliated retail leadership, preferably in passenger car segment.Minimum 8–10 years in a CEO / Business Head / General Manager capacity with full P&L ownership.Exposure to PHEV, NEV, EV or new-technology vehicle retail operations strongly preferred.Proven track record of leading a multi-outlet, multi-brand or high-volume dealership group.

3. Key Responsibilities

1. Business Strategy & P&L Ownership

2. Sales, Aftersales & Cross-Functional Operations Oversight

3. OEM & Key Stakeholder Relationship Management

4. New Energy Vehicle (PHEV/NEV) Business Readiness & Charging Infrastructure

5. Financial Planning, Working Capital & Investment Management

6. Talent Leadership & Organization Development

7. Facility, Infrastructure & Regulatory Compliance

8. Customer Experience & Brand Standards Governance

4. Key Performance Indicators (KPIs)

i. Business Performance
  • Overall dealership net profitability (%)
  • Revenue growth across sales, aftersales, F&I and VAS
  • Return on capital employed (ROCE)
  • Market share within territory
ii. Sales & Aftersales Effectiveness
  • Sales target achievement (volume & value)
  • Service throughput and bay/workshop utilization
  • PHEV/NEV charging infrastructure readiness & uptime
iii. Customer Experience
  • Sales Satisfaction Index (SSI)
  • Net Promoter Score (NPS)
  • Customer complaint resolution turnaround time
iv. Financial Health
  • Working capital and inventory turnaround days
  • Debtor days and OEM claims/incentive realization
v. People & Governance
  • Leadership team retention and bench strength
  • Statutory, OEM audit and process compliance score

5. Key Competencies

Strategic & Business AcumenP&L OwnershipOEM & Stakeholder ManagementPeople LeadershipChange Management (EV/NEV Transition)Financial AcumenCustomer CentricityDecision Making & Risk Management

Position Overview

The Business Head / CEO owns the dealership's overall P&L and strategic direction, leading sales, aftersales, and value-added business functions to deliver profitable growth, brand governance, and long-term stakeholder value in a vehicle retail environment. This position is at DP level.

1. Education

Graduate / MBA in Business Administration, Management, Engineering or related field.Additional certification in Automotive Retail Management or General Management preferred.

2. Experience

18–25 years of experience in automotive dealership operations or OEM-affiliated retail leadership, preferably in passenger car segment.Minimum 8–10 years in a CEO / Business Head / General Manager capacity with full P&L ownership.Exposure to PHEV, NEV, EV or new-technology vehicle retail operations strongly preferred.Proven track record of leading a multi-outlet, multi-brand or high-volume dealership group.

3. Key Responsibilities

1. Business Strategy & P&L Ownership

2. Sales, Aftersales & Cross-Functional Operations Oversight

3. OEM & Key Stakeholder Relationship Management

4. New Energy Vehicle (PHEV/NEV) Business Readiness & Charging Infrastructure

7. Facility, Infrastructure & Regulatory Compliance

8. Customer Experience & Brand Standards Governance

4. Key Performance Indicators (KPIs)

i. Business Performance
  • Overall dealership net profitability (%)
  • Revenue growth across sales, aftersales, F&I and VAS
  • Return on capital employed (ROCE)
  • Market share within territory
ii. Sales & Aftersales Effectiveness
  • Sales target achievement (volume & value)
  • Service throughput and bay/workshop utilization
  • PHEV/NEV charging infrastructure readiness & uptime
iii. Customer Experience
  • Sales Satisfaction Index (SSI)
  • Net Promoter Score (NPS)
  • Customer complaint resolution turnaround time
iv. Financial Health
  • Working capital and inventory turnaround days
  • Debtor days and OEM claims/incentive realization
v. People & Governance
  • Leadership team retention and bench strength
  • Statutory, OEM audit and process compliance score

5. Key Competencies

Strategic & Business AcumenP&L OwnershipOEM & Stakeholder ManagementPeople LeadershipChange Management (EV/NEV Transition)Financial AcumenCustomer CentricityDecision Making & Risk Management

CHAPTER 2

Dealership Organisation Structure

OBJECTIVE:

To provide dealer partners with a recommended reporting structure that is right sized for their outlet category, so accountability is clear and manpower is as required.

CUSTOMER IMPACT:

A right-sized, well-structured team means customers are attended to promptly at every touchpoint, without gaps caused by unclear reporting lines or missing roles.

A dealership runs on people. If reporting lines are unclear, jobs get missed, customers wait longer, and no one owns the outcome.

Why this structure is required

01every customer touchpoint has an owner and a manager behind it
02escalations go to the right person
03new hires learn their role and reporting line quickly

    Functional reporting vs. operational coordination

    Functional reporting (solid line)

    The person this employee works for.

    Operational coordination (dashed line)

    A working relationship the employee must maintain to do the job.

     Functional reportingOperational coordination
    Sets goals and KPIsYesNo, but may be consulted
    Conducts the reviewYesProvides input to the functional manager
    Approves leaveYesNo
    Directs day-to-day workYesOnly within the agreed area of coordination
    Initiates disciplinary actionYesNo, raises it with the functional manager
    CHAPTER 3

    Recruitment and Selection

    "Don't hire for only skills, hire for attitude."
    OBJECTIVE:

    To ensure the dealership has the right people in the right roles through smart recruiting, assessment and onboarding.

    CUSTOMER IMPACT:

    Right people in the right role, and in sufficient quantity enhances the Customer Journey by delivering better experience.

    Principles

    • Hire on knowledge, skill and attitude (refer 3A. Candidate Evaluation Sheet).
    • No discrimination or hiring below the age of 18 years.
    • Promote internal mobility before external hiring.
    • Anti-poaching - consult JSW area office before contacting any fellow JSW dealership partner employee.

    3.2 Recruitment Need and Sourcing

    • Recruitment need can arise in two cases for which you will need to use form 3B. as mentioned in the above flowchart:
    • Proactive recruitment: For new manpower requirement. As per the volume norms shared by JSW Motors, calculate the no. of positions required.
    • Reactive recruitment: For backfill positions where a vacancy is due to the employee’s exit or internal movement.
    • Internal movement covers promotion, lateral transfer between roles, and transfer between outlets of the same dealership. The HR Manager must explore the following routes before external sourcing:
    SourceCost effectivenessSpeed of hiringCandidate qualitySuitable for
    Internal job postingHighFastHighAll roles. Post every vacancy internally before going outside.
    PromotionHighVariableHighTeam Leader, Sales Manager and other roles with a ready internal successor
    Lateral movementHighFastModerateMovement between customer facing and support roles
    Manpower poolHighFastVariableCustomer facing and support roles hired in numbers
    Former employeesHighFastHighAll roles, subject to exit interview records

    Cost effectiveness, speed and quality are indicative.

    • Use 3C. Internal Job Posting (IJP) Template to notify the position internally. Note that every internal and external candidate will have to go through the recruitment process listed in the above flowchart.
    EligibilityHow to apply
    • Completed 18 months in the current role
    • Not under a performance improvement plan
    • No live disciplinary case
    • Check the Internal Job postings from the HR
    • Inform your current reporting manager
    • Share filled up 3D. Internal Job Posting Application Form with the HR

    Employee referral programme

    Who may refer

    • All confirmed employees may refer candidates for any open position.
    • Employees on probation may refer. The payout is released after their own confirmation.
    • The HR Manager, the HR Executive and anybody on the interview panel for that position may not claim a bonus for it. They may still refer; the referral simply carries no payment.
    • The Dealer Principal and the Business Head may not claim referral bonuses.

    Referring a family member is permitted but is governed by the following guardrails:

    • Mandatory relationship disclosure
    • Selection will be on merit as per assessment criteria
    • Salary and compensation has to be as per company norms
    • Relatives should not be in the same team
    Referring A Family Member: The Guardrails
    01
    Mandatory relationship disclosure
    02
    Selection on merit, per assessment criteria
    03
    Salary & comp as per company norms
    04
    Relatives should not be in the same team

    How it works

    • The referring employee submits the 3F. Employee referral form with the CV to HR.
    • The referrer cannot be a part of the selection process.
    • Both the referrer and the person referred must be in service on the date of payout.
    • Payment is made through payroll and is subject to tax deduction.

    • As a next step in screening, run the resume through the AI tool to generate a suitability score.
    • Shortlisted candidate receives a link from HR Manager to log-in to the recruitment portal.
    • The candidate then uploads CV, DL & Photo in the recruitment portal for verification.
    • Once the documents are uploaded, the HR managers receives the entry on the portal and approves it. This triggers an online assessment containing 15 psychometric evaluation questions with 80% weightage and 5 questions on video-based AI interaction with 20% weightage.
    • Post completion of the assessment, a report is generated by the tool. The HR Manager approves candidates with >=60% aggregate score.
    • This triggers a message to undergo interview round 1. A panel of HR and SM/GM or the reporting manager conducts the interview 1 in-person at the dealership and enters the score online.
    • Upon passing interview round 1, an auto-message is triggered notifying the candidate to undergo round 2. A panel of HR and ASM (RM of managerial roles) conducts interview 2 in-person or virtually and enters the score online.
    • After undergoing round 1 and round 2 interviews, a consolidated approval/rejection report is generated.
    • The reporting manager must check the following before taking hiring decision:
    FactorWhat to check
    Salary bracketExpectation against the approved band for the role
    Desire for growthWhat the candidate wants to be doing in two years
    Distance and commuteDistance from the outlet and how they will travel each day
    Notice periodJoining date against the date the position is needed
    Working patternWillingness to work weekends, festivals and month-ends
    LanguageLocal language ability for the market the outlet serves
    Licence and drivingValid licence and actual driving ability
    Employment stabilityThe reason behind each job change, not the tenure alone
    Reference checkThe outcome, including any note raised
    Anti-poachingWhether the candidate is with another JSW dealer partner
    Team fitWho the candidate will report to and work within the team

    3.4 Reference checks and background verification

    Reference check and background verification is done in-house by the HR Manager OR through an outsourced partner (refer 3G. Reference check form and 3H. Background verification form).

    What is verified

    CheckDocument and method
    IdentityAadhaar, PAN, passport or voter identity card
    AddressAadhaar, utility bill, rent agreement or bank statement
    EducationDegree certificate and mark sheet for the highest qualification
    Previous employmentRelieving letter, last three salary slips and appointment letter from the most recent employer
    Reference checkPhone conversation with two references, at least one a previous supervisor
    Driving licenceValid licence for the class of vehicle, with the expiry date recorded
    Police verificationThrough the local police station or a licensed agency. Recommended for Cashier, Driver, Security, Pantry and Housekeeping.
    Bank accountCancelled cheque or passbook copy in the employee’s own name
    Medical certificateA medical fitness report must be provided before date of joining.

    3.5 Recruitment KPIs

    The following KPIs for the HR department helps in assessing its efficiency:

    KPIHow it is calculatedRecommended target
    Average recruitment cycle time
    • Average of = (Date of offer acceptance – Date of approved requisition to HR) for the last 3 months
    • Example:

    • Middle: 30 days
    • Senior: 60 days
    • Role categories are listed below.

    LevelRoles
    JuniorSales Consultant, Corporate Sales Executive, Used Car Consultant, Accessories Sales Executive, CRE Sales, Delivery Coordinator, Receptionist, Hostess, Driver / Valet, Security, Car Registration and Delivery Executive (Sales Admin), Marketing Executive, Test Drive Coordinator, Housekeeping, Pantry Team, Cashier
    MiddleSales Team Leader, Car Finance Executive, Car Insurance Executive, Car Evaluator, CRM Sales, Internal Dealer Trainer, Digital Engagement Manager, Accountant, HR Executive / Admin, EDP Executive

    3.6 Impact of manpower attrition

    An exit costs more than just the loss of retail.

    Worked example: a Sales Team Leader with three Sales Consultants

    What is lostWhyIndicative loss
    Team productivityTeam output drops while the position is vacant and the consultants work without daily supervisionFrom earlier 5 to now 2 vehicles per consultant per month
    Own retailThe Team Leader carries a personal retail number that nobody takes overFull monthly retail of one Team Leader
    Lead pipelineSix months of leads held by the Team Leader go cold, along with the cost spent on generating each leadLeads carried x cost per lead
    Replacement costSourcing cost, consultancy fee or referral payout, plus induction and training before the replacement is productiveCost per hire + training cost
    Ramp-up timeA new Team Leader takes about three months to reach full productivityThree months of partial output

    How to calculate the cost of an exit

    • Vacancy loss = (monthly team retail before the exit - monthly team retail during the vacancy) x months vacant x average gross margin per vehicle
    • Pipeline loss = number of open leads held x cost per lead
    • Replacement cost = sourcing cost + referral or agency payout + induction and training cost
    • Ramp-up loss = shortfall against target during the ramp-up period x average gross margin per vehicle

    Total cost of one exit = vacancy loss + pipeline loss + replacement cost + ramp-up loss

    Note: the multipliers above are indicative. Each dealership should replace them with its own productivity, margin and cost-per-lead figures.

    3.7 Best Practices

    • Keep a live manpower list of position-wise, screened candidates. These can be:
      • Candidates who could not move to the next rounds for various reasons. Mention the reason.
      • Explore this internal pool whenever a new opening comes up.
    • Refer to an accurate JD with correct responsibilities, KPIs, and competencies while starting the recruitment process.
    • Agree the salary band and the approval route before contacting candidates.
    • Follow the entire selection process even when the position is urgent.
    • Check the reasons behind short tenures in the CV rather than rejecting on tenure alone.
    • Complete reference checks before the offer, not after.
    • Tell every candidate the outcome, including those who are not selected.
    • Where a candidate does not join, mention the reason coping the reporting manager on email.
    • Candidate data copies are held securely, and are not shared outside the dealership except where the law requires it.
    • Original documents must be returned the same day.
    • Documents of unsuccessful candidates are held for six months with consent.
    • Where any manpower come via an agency, obtain written confirmation that their identity and police verification has been done.

    CHAPTER 4

    Learning and Development

    4. Learning and Development
    “Training is not an expense, but an investment in human capital”
    OBJECTIVE:

    To identify capability gaps, provide relevant training, measure learning effectiveness and continuously improve employee performance.

    CUSTOMER IMPACT:

    Continuous training at JSW Motors ensures customers receive accurate product information, professional handling and a consistent experience across all touchpoints.

    JSW Motors and the dealership together build the learning ecosystem at a dealership.

    JSW Motors provides:

    • The Learning Management System (LMS)
    • A curriculum mapped to each role, along with the competency framework
    • The learner journey and its levels
    • Certification assessments and outcomes

    The dealership is responsible for:

    • Preparing people for the certification assessments
    • Making sure the JSW defined behaviours and processes are exhibited on the floor
    • Make continuous improvement in Customer Experience by developing new joinees, and improving capability of the existing manpower

    The HR Manager owns Learning and Development at the dealership, supported by the Internal Dealer Trainer (IDT). This chapter sets out the training principles and how the HR Manager and the IDT run the governance.

    Principles

    • No manpower without induction training is on the floor
    • No less than level 1 certified people interact with the customers
    • No deviation of competency pathway in increments or promotions
    • If KPIs are not met, then retraining is necessary
    • Failure to attend training impacts employee’s appraisal

    4.1 Joining and Induction Training

    Induction is the first training a new joiner receives. It is completed within 1 week of joining and is run by the IDT with the HR Manager.

    How induction is run

    In the first week:

    • Day 1 - The IDT enrols the new joiner on the LMS and confirms the induction courses list.
    • Day 1 - A buddy is assigned by the HR Manager who the new joiner can interact with.
    • For the first two weeks the new joiner shadows the buddy through complete customer interactions.
    • Day 2 - The reporting manager discusses the roles & responsibilities and the KPIs.
    • Day 3 and 4 – Observe buddy handling the customers and do the assigned induction training.
    • Day 5 - Performance management goals are set with the reporting manager.
    • Day 6 - HR records induction completion in the training record.

    Monthly training calendar

    The IDT builds a training calendar for the following month by 25th and the Dealer Principal approves it. It is put on the notice board and shared by email.

    In order to do the training need analysis, the IDT must follow the below workflow:

    On top of these JSW driven trainings, there will be other trainings that the IDT must include in its training calendar:

    • Daily - 15 mins enjoyable roleplay session run by the reporting manager during the morning meeting with a topic, chosen from what actually went wrong like a lost deal, a complaint, or a new scheme.
    • Weekly - a standard one-hour classroom training conducted by the reporting manager or IDT to cover the following suggested topics:
    • Monthly – competition mystery shops of nearby dealerships to understand the competitor ecosystem. Discuss the findings in the morning meeting lead by the reporting manager.
    • Regular refresher training conducted by the IDT on JSW prescribed topics.

    When someone is absent

    It should be the responsibility of the dealership to send the nominated employees for training. Per participant training cost will be debited by JSW in case of their uninformed absence.

    • Attendance is recorded for every training session by the IDT in the calendar sheet or the LMS.
    • A person who cannot attend informs the reporting manager and the IDT at least 2 days in advance (except for emergency cases) and is scheduled into the next session.
    • A no-show at a JSW programme wastes a seat and is reported to the manager.
    • Repeated absence without reason is handled as a breach of discipline and conduct.

    When someone fails an assessment

    • For LMS e-learnings, retake is allowed on the platform.
    • The certificate is not awarded until the assigned course assessment is not cleared.
    • For classroom trainings, if anyone has failed the post-test, they will have to undertake the training again in the next round in order to get certified.
    • Classroom training first attempt at each level failed - reassessment in the next training round.
    • Classroom training second attempt at each level failed - the reporting manager joins the conversation, and a development plan is agreed, with a date.
    • Classroom training third attempt at each level failed - the Business Head reviews whether this is the right role for the person.

    4.3 Using the LMS

    [PLACEHOLDER SECTION: NEED FUNCTIONALITY AND LMS DETAILS]

    The LMS provided by JSW Motors holds the course library, the learner journey and the training record for every employee.

    • The IDT creates the login on day one of joining and assigns the courses at each level one by one.
    • The IDT checks LMS progress weekly and flags the missed due dates to the reporting manager.
    • Assessment results and certification status flow from the LMS into the training record.
    • Where a person changes role, the IDT updates the role mapping so the correct curriculum is assigned.

    4.5 Best Practices

    • Use real situations from your own floor during training.
    • Make people practise in front of each other.
    • Keep sessions short.
    • Watch people with actual customers before certifying them.
    • Release your people for training as per calendar.
    • Coach on the floor, every day.
    • IDT must prepare a monthly skill contest and the HR must run it via the LMS.
    • IDT must publish a monthly learning leaderboard on the notice board with scores on courses completed, assessment results and certifications earned.
    • Announce certifications the same way as sales achievements during morning meetings.

    CHAPTER 5

    Performance Management

    5. Performance Management
    “The key to successful performance management is to focus on the future, not the past. It’s about enabling and empowering employees, not just evaluating them.”
    OBJECTIVE:

    To review employee’s contribution fairly and consistently against agreed goals and good performance to be recognised, gaps to be addressed before they affect the business.

    CUSTOMER IMPACT:

    Regular, fair performance reviews keep employees focused on their job responsibilities and KPIs and ultimately impact the customer experience.

    Principles

    • Follow the financial year for performance review cycle.
    • Only measurable goals must be set against the target KPIs as per the dealership annual target plan.
    • Feedbacks are provided frequently, not saved for only the performance review day.

    5.1 Performance management cycle

    Five fixed points in the appraisal cycle.

    StepStageWhat happens
    1Goal settingSMART goals for the cycle are agreed and signed by the reporting manager and the employee.
    2Quarterly reviewOne-on-one on progress against the agreed goals, recorded on email.
    3Mid-year reviewFormal check on progress, feedback and course correction.
    4Annual appraisalSelf-assessment, manager assessment, rating and review meeting.
    5Increment and promotionRatings are applied to increment and promotion decisions.

    5.2 Performance management process

    The eleven steps of the cycle, and who owns each one.

    Chart 5.2 Performance management process

    5.3 Setting goals

    Step 01 – Annual target planning by the top management

    Step 02 – Reporting manager to define the KPIs target with for each individual using 5A. KPIs Laundry List

    Step 03 – Discuss the KPIs with employees and set the expectations

    Step 04 – Formal documentation of KPIs and submission to the HR

    Step 05 – Write the goals for the particular appraisal cycle using 5B. Goal Setting and KPI Sheet and define each goal’s weightage.

    The SMART Goal Framework
    SMART
    S
    Specific — exactly what to accomplish
    M
    Measurable — how success is measured
    A
    Achievable — realistic with resources
    R
    Relevant — aligns with objectives
    T
    Time-bound — a clear deadline

    The goals and weightage must be written in 5C. Performance Review Form (Quarterly, Mid-year and Annual). See example below:

    GoalKPI / measureTargetWeightage %
    Achieve average monthly vehicle retail of 5 for the current yearBooking to retail ratio100%50%
    Achieve average accessory penetration value of INR xxxx by the end of this yearAccessory penetration100%30%
    Convert 60% of my retails to dealership finance by the end of Q4Finance penetration60%20%

    Follow the SMART framework while writing a goal:

    • S – Specific – exactly what you want to accomplish
    • M – Measurable – how success will be measured
    • A – Achievable – realistic with available resources
    • R – Relevant – goal aligns with broader objectives
    • T – Time-bound – set a clear deadline for completion

    Examples:

    Weak goalSMART goal for a Sales ConsultantWhat makes it SMART
    Improve customer satisfactionKeep my customer satisfaction score at 90% or above in every month of the appraisal cycle.
    • S – one score, on my own customers.
    • M – 90% or above, taken from the monthly satisfaction report.
    • A – my score last cycle was 85%, so five points is within reach.
    • R – customer satisfaction is a dealership KPI.
    • T – measured every month through the cycle.
    Increase finance penetrationConvert 60% of my retails to dealership finance by the end of the appraisal cycle.
    • S – dealership finance on my own retails.
    • M – 60% of retails, tracked in the DMS.
    • A – I am at 45% today and the showroom average is 62%.
    • R – finance penetration is a dealership profit line.
    • T – by the end of the cycle, reviewed each quarter.
    Do more test drivesGive a test drive to 70% of my walk-in enquiries every month through the appraisal cycle.
    • S – test drives on my own walk-in enquiries.
    • M – 70%, counted from the enquiry record in the CRM.
    • A – I am at 55% now, which is about two more test drives a week.
    • R – test drives lift the enquiry to booking conversion.
    • T – every month through the cycle.

    5.4 Quarterly and mid-year review

    • HR should notify the reporting managers about the Mid-Year Review meeting.
    • Reporting manager schedules a one on one mid year review meeting.
    • Review performance expectations against the set goals.
    • Where each goal stands, in numbers.
    • What is going well, said plainly and specifically.
    • What has to change in the next six months, and what support the person needs to do it.
    • Whether any goal needs revising because the ground shifted.
    • Reporting manager shares 5C. Performance Review Form (Quarterly, Mid-year and Annual) with the employees with the HR Manager in cc.
    • Document what was agreed on an email with the HR Manager in cc summarize meeting conclusions about:
    • Progress
    • Favourable Results
    • Performance Issues/Problems Solutions
    • Agreements and Commitments

    5.5 The annual appraisal and ratings

    4Exceeds expectationsPerformance is consistently better than the agreed goal.
    3Meets expectationsGoal is achieved as expected.
    2Needs improvementFalls short, needs a written plan and support.

    • Steps for Annual Appraisal will be same as the Mid Year Review process.
    • The manager rates, the Business Head reviews, the Dealer Principal approves while the HR runs the process and keeps it fair.
    • A minimum rating of 3 is required for promotion, and no rating below 3 in the past two years.
    • A rating of 2 or below means a written improvement plan and no increment that year.
    • A rating of 1 goes to the process in 5.6.
    • Nobody can be rated 4 or 5 if they have an open disciplinary matter or an integrity concern.

    5.7 Best practices

    • Manager must link individual goals to dealership priorities by explaining how each goal contributes to dealership performance.
    • Ratings and feedback should be supported by KPI results, customer feedback, quality checks, attendance records, and work completed.
    • Quarterly, Mid-year and Annual reviews must be concluded with clear development actions such as coaching, product & process training, exposure to additional responsibilities.
    • Every appraisal form is signed (or email acknowledged) by the employee, and the manager.
    • HR Manager reports the rating spread by department to the Dealer Principal each year.
    • Someone who changes role mid-cycle gets new goals for the new role.
    • Someone with less than three months in the role at the end of appraisal cycle is not rated. Their manager records a short note instead in performance review form.

    CHAPTER 6

    Career Progression

    "Train people well enough so they can leave. Treat them well enough so they don't want to."
    OBJECTIVE:

    To give employees a visible and achievable path for growth within the dealership, so good performers stay motivated and are retained.

    CUSTOMER IMPACT:

    Long retained employees bring better value in terms of product and customer knowledge. This helps subsequently drive customer experience.

    This chapter talks about the different career possibilities people can explore at JSW Motors dealership. The aim is to provide employees with a clear and achievable growth path within the dealership, helping them stay motivated and build a long-term career.

    6.1 Career progression routes

    These are the usual career progression paths at a dealership and can be followed if there is a vacancy. Note that the time for movement to a new role is only for guidance.

    Chart 6.1 Career routes at a JSW Motors dealership. Note: This is the table for the same work area movement. Lateral movement is also possible which is explained further in this chapter

    6.2 Requirements for career progression

    The requirementHow it is checked
    1Time spent in the current role
    • Minimum 18 months
    • Only Confirmed employees should be considered
    2Performance
    • Rating of 3 or more in the last annual review and no rating below 3 in the past two years.
    • No pending integrity or disciplinary action
    3Competency for the next roleAssessed against the skills and competencies of the new role
    4Certification
    • All the required training levels should be completed for the current role
    • The leadership trainings completed before any people-managing role

    Qualities We Look for in Future People Leaders

    Competencies alone may not be sufficient for a good people leader. Following are some of the personality traits that are important to note while promoting someone to people leader position.

    • Kind and helpful
    • Integrity and empathy
    • Accountability and fairness
    • Coaching mindset
    • Humility and approachability
    • Clear and effective communication skills
    • Earns the respect of the team through their actions, behaviour, and leadership
    Qualities Of Future People Leaders
    Kind and helpful
    Integrity and empathy
    Accountability and fairness
    Coaching mindset
    Humility and approachability
    Clear, effective communication
    Earns the team's respect through action

    If someone does not demonstrate most of these qualities, they may still perform very well in their current role. In such cases, consider providing opportunities for growth through a larger area of responsibility, a specialist career path, or enhanced rewards and recognition.

    6.3 Promotion process

    Promotions are decided at the annual review, alongside increments, unless a vacancy comes up mid-year.

    6.4 Cross department movements

    The process is the same as a promotion, except the minimum tenure requirement does not apply. If an employee is not in the right role, they should not have to wait 18 months to move.

    The table below lists some examples of lateral movement:

    MoveWhy it often works
    CRE Sales to Sales ConsultantThey already have an understanding of the products, process and customer base. They also know how to identify and handle customer concerns effectively.
    Car Finance or Car Insurance to Sales Consultant or Sales Team LeaderThey look beyond their own enquiries and understand the overall business and sales performance of the dealership.
    Sales Consultant to Corporate SalesSuits somebody who is patient, organised and skilled at building strong relationships over time.
    Sales Consultant or Team Leader to Internal Dealer TrainerThe credibility to train comes from having sold. This is the natural source for the role.
    Delivery Coordinator to Sales AdminSame documents, same discipline, a wider view of the process.
    Hostess or Receptionist to CRE SalesA common and successful first step for somebody who is good with people and wants more responsibility.

    6.5 Best Practices

    • Employees are given the first opportunity to apply for vacant positions before external sourcing begins.
    • A promotion can take place only if there is an available role that has been approved as part of the dealership's manpower plan.
    • All applicants who are not chosen for a role will be informed of the outcome and provided with feedback by their manager within seven days.
    • Employees who transfer to another outlet within the same dealer partner will retain their length of service, leave balance, and job grade.
    • Career development discussions should take place regularly as part of performance management and be properly documented. Employees and managers should regularly discuss future career aspirations and development opportunities.

    CHAPTER 7

    Compensation, Benefits and Incentive Policy

    7. Compensation, Benefits and Incentive Policy
    "Paying good wages is not charity at all – it is the best kind of business."
    OBJECTIVE:

    To ensure pay and benefits are structured fairly and competitively. This is important to attract and retain the right talent.

    CUSTOMER IMPACT:

    Fair and competitive compensation helps the dealership retain better talent, so customers are served by people who understand the brand, the process and their needs.

    This chapter suggests how employee salary should be structured as per industry norms and the benefits that go along with it.

    The HR Manager is responsible (in consultation with the dealer Leadership Team) for setting the salary structure based on the local market and what the business can afford.

    Principles

    • Pay salary on the 5th day of every month.
    • Follow all statutory requirements, including Provident Fund, ESIC, gratuity and bonus.
    • Salary is confidential to an employee and should be known to HR, the reporting manager and the employee.
    • Keep a pay-for-performance component in the compensation.
    • Salary should be benchmarked with current market trends every year.

    7.1 Components of Salary

    Total compensation has three parts. Everyone in the dealership gets the first two. The third depends on the role, market conditions and periodic performance in the role.

    PartWhat it includes
    Fixed payBasic salary, dearness allowance, house rent allowance, and any other regular allowance, performance allowance based on rolled out policy
    Statutory benefitsProvident Fund, ESIC or medical insurance, gratuity, bonus, and paid leave
    Variable payMonthly or quarterly incentive, linked to performance.

    7.5 Incentive Policy

    Performance Incentive plays an important role in achieving the short term and long term goals of the JSW Dealership organization.

    This section covers the incentive policy applicable to the Dealership Organization only, and doesn’t account for the JSW incentive schemes.

    Some guiding principles –

    • As explained in 7.2, the incentive policy is the component within variable pay of the salary component. The salary for the month “n” will have the incentive for the “n-1” month
    • For JSW Motors, as it is building its brand, bookings is equally important as retail for building momentum, while designing the Sales team incentive structure (as explained in the sample monthly incentive scheme)
    • As we move forward, JSW Motors will emphasize on Incentive schemes for Allied Business and some more CX parameters
    • Monthly incentive scheme to be designed by the 25th of every month, and released to all staff on the first working day of next month.
    • The monthly incentive scheme payout should be calculated for the “n-1” month by the 3rd of every month, so that salary including incentive amount can be paid by 5th of every month
    • Incentive paid on time only, will have positive impact on target achievement as desired

    7.6 Timelines for Compensation, Benefits and Incentive Processing Workflow

    DateMonthActivityWho Does ItSupported By
    25thn-1Monthly incentive scheme finalizedHR ManagerManagement / HR
    1stnScheme communicated to all employeesHR ManagerHR
    1st-3rdnPerformance validation and payout calculation for the n-1 monthHR ManagerHR & Finance
    5thnSalary and incentive payoutHR ManagerPayroll / Finance

    7.7 Best Practices

    For JSW Motors India, the incentive process should not just be timely, but should actively support the brand's current growth stage, network expansion, and retail momentum. Here are some precise best practices suitable for inclusion in the policy deck.

    1. Balance Bookings and Retails :

    • Incentive schemes should reward both confirmed bookings and retail deliveries.
    • Cancelled booking needs to be taken out in next month

    2. Publish the Incentive Scheme on the First Day of the Month:

    • All signed-off schemes should be released on the first working day of the next month. Mid-month target changes should be avoided.

    3. Keep Monthly Schemes Simple :

    • Limit incentive calculations to a maximum of 3-4 performance parameters.
    • Sales consultants should be able to estimate their own earnings without requiring HR or Finance support.

    4. Link Incentives to Business Priority :

    • Introduce model-wise boosters for vehicles identified as strategic priorities by JSW Motors. Additional incentives may be offered for EV variants, newly launched products, or slow-moving inventory.

    5. Pay Incentives Along with Salary

    • Incentives should always be processed as part of the monthly salary cycle. Delayed payouts reduce the motivational impact of the scheme.

    6. Protect New Joiners and New Dealerships

    • New sales consultants should receive a realistic ramp-up target for the first 60-90 days.
    • New dealerships may operate under a simplified incentive structure until market demand stabilizes.

    CHAPTER 8

    Employee Engagement, Rewards and Recognition

    8. Employee Engagement, Rewards and Recognition
    "People work for money, but go the extra mile for recognition, praise, and rewards."
    OBJECTIVE:

    To build a culture where good work is noticed and appreciated regularly, so employees feel valued beyond their monthly pay cheque.

    CUSTOMER IMPACT:

    Employees who feel appreciated bring more energy and care to their interactions, which customers notice and respond to positively.

    Financial remuneration alone is not the prime driver of motivation and employee retention. Employee engagement and recognition in the role through appreciation, monitory rewards, rewards in kind, awards and certificates, are small but important aspects to drive employee motivation and competitive ecosystem. A well-designed rewards and recognition policy is a must in today’s world.

    Following principles to be followed while designing the Engagement Programs :

    • Engagement drives should involve all role holders of the dealership (imbibed around the JSW Philosophy of shared future)
    • Engagement drives should be year around and should be distributed evenly
    • Dealer Leadership participation is must

    Following principles to be followed while designing the Rewards and Recognition Programs :

        • Recognize actions reflecting JSW values
    • Reward behaviours that delight customers.
    • Celebrate individual and team achievements.
    • Encourage learning, growth, and improvement.
    • Link rewards to measurable business outcomes.
    • Promote transparency, inclusion, and respect.
    • R&R Programs are open to all

    CHAPTER 9

    Employee Lifecycle Management

    9. Employee Lifecycle Management
    "Belonging is not the same thing as feeling like you fit in. Belonging is when you feel valued for everything that makes you stand out."
    OBJECTIVE:

    To ensure every stage of an employee's journey - from joining to exit - is handled consistently and professionally, so employees have a positive experience and the dealership stays compliant throughout.

    CUSTOMER IMPACT:

    A well-managed lifecycle, from onboarding to exit, ensures customers always deal with employees who are properly inducted, informed and prepared.

    This chapter covers the whole journey of a person at the dealership from the day they join to the day they may leave.

    Principles

    • No employee starts work without completing the required joining formalities
    • Confirmation, growth & career opportunities are based on performance & capability
    • Every employee’s movement and separation is managed through process and approvals
    • Exits are handled professionally with complete handover and closure

    9.1 Joining

    Joining process

    9.2 Confirmation

    The recommended probation period is six months.

    The three possible outcomes

    OutcomeWhenWhat follows
    ConfirmedDoing the job, training complete, no conduct problemConfirmation letter issued. The person becomes eligible for referral bonus, salary advance, IJP (Internal job posting) and the full leave entitlement.

    Notice period

    StageNotice Period
    During probation15 days
    After confirmation, Customer Facing and Support roles30 days
    After confirmation, Leadership roles60 days
    • Notice can be shortened by mutual agreement, in writing.
    • Notice can be bought out by the employee or next employer, or waived by the dealership, but the decision must be approved & recorded.
    • Leave cannot be taken during notice period unless taken with manager’s agreement for emergencies.

    9.4 Handover & Exit Interview

    • The handover should include the transfer of key responsibilities, ongoing tasks, current deliverables status, critical contacts, important documentation, ending actions to designated employee or Manager.
    • Knowledge transfer session to be conducted to ensure the receiving employee effectively assumes responsibilities to minimize operational risks.
    • Return or transfer ownership of company assets.
    • Both sides sign the handover form.
    • System access is removed on the last working day.

    Exit interview

    An exit interview gives an opportunity to share feedback on overall employment experience. It is to be done by the HR Manager in the last week around the following lines:

    • Reason for leaving
    • About the role & Manager in terms of expectations, support & guidance
    • About the work environment
    • About the growth & development
    • About compensation and benefits
    • Preference for come back, and recommendation to friends & Colleagues
    • Open Feedback

    HR should read all the exit interviews together and look for a pattern and share the findings with the Dealer Principal.

    9.5 Full and Final Settlement

    • Salary dues must be settled within 2 weeks.
    • Gratuity, where payable, is released within 30 days.
    • Provident Fund is claimed by the employee and HR can help with the paperwork.
    • Earned incentive for tenure completed months is paid as part of full and final settlement.
    • Any advance or dues are adjusted.
    • The relieving letter and experience letter are given as soon as the settlement is done.

    Best Practice

    • Create a memorable first impression for every new joiner with workplace arrangement
    • Invest dedicated time with every new joiner during first week
    • Discuss periodically with high performing employees to strengthen engagement. Offer vacancies internally before going outside.
    • Recognize and celebrate key employee milestones – confirmation, certification, promotions, service anniversaries.
    • Utilize exit interview insights by analyzing feedback and implementing actions.

    CHAPTER 10

    Discipline and Conduct

    10. Discipline and Conduct
    "Talent might make you good but it’s your attitude and work ethic that will make you great."
    OBJECTIVE:

    The professional image of JSW motors is directly linked to the way each individual present themselves and behave. Set out clear standards of workplace behaviour and a fair process for addressing misconduct, so issues are handled consistently and employees know what is expected of them.

    CUSTOMER IMPACT:

    A disciplined dealership environment encourages professionalism in every customer interaction. Customer gets fair treatment, timely responses and reliable service leading to trust in JSW brand.

    Principles

    • Be honest, transparent and ethical in every decision, transaction and interaction
    • Respect people & diversity
    • Be accountable for your actions
    • Protect trust and confidentiality
    • Promote a safe and compliant workplace

    Every organisation has their own DNA and ways of doing things. At JSW, (OEM and franchise partners included) we are governed by our pillars of foundation. They include our vision, our behaviours to execute that vision and work ethics. All of this together brings out the essence of working at JSW and supporting our customers.

    Our code of conduct and expected behavioural etiquettes are framed based on the above. These principles as explained below not only define how we work but will take us far into our individual journey as a human being.

    10.1 Code of conduct

    a. Purpose & Scope The following code of Conduct applies to all the retail partner and its employees and sets out the ethical and behavioural requirement that are mandatory. The Code of Conduct is a necessary component to maintain the integrity of JSW brand and guarantee that customers continue to trust us.

    b. Ethical Business & Sales Practices

    Transparency: Be honest about prices, vehicle specs, financing terms, and warranties. There shall be no Hidden fees, deceptive payment, and misleading advertising.

    Allied Business Transactions: Do only authorized accessories fitment, merchandise sales. Give correct written estimates before further fitment and delivery.

    Data Privacy: Ensure that customer personal and financial data is protected. Process credit applications, ID and contact information in compliance with local laws on privacy.

    c. Professional and Behavioural Traits

    Customer First: Treat every visitor with utmost courtesy, responsiveness, and professionalism, irrespective of their buying intentions or abilities.

    Brand Representation: Maintain showroom and staff appearance consistent with JSW brand visual identity guidelines.

    d. Equal Opportunity & Fair Workplace

    Zero Tolerance for Discrimination: Promote diversity and inclusion by providing equal opportunity in hiring, promotion, and daily operations without regard to race, gender, religion, age, sexual orientation, or disability.

    Safe Environment: Maintain a workplace free from harassment (including sexual harassment), bullying, and intimidation.

    Fair Compensation: Comply with all local labour laws, ensuring fair & timely wages and safe working conditions for all dealership staff.

    e. Anti-Corruption & Compliance

    Bribery & Kickbacks: Do not offer, give, solicit, or accept bribes, kickbacks, or inappropriate gifts from customers, suppliers, lenders, or government officials.

    Conflicts of Interest: Disclose any personal or financial relationships that might influence business decisions or give an unfair business advantage.

    Legal Adherence: Comply fully with all local automotive, consumer protection, environmental, and financial regulations.

    f. Reporting & Enforcement

    Duty to Report: Employees must promptly report any suspected violations of this Code to the HR Manager or through the organisation’s anonymous compliance policy/channel.

    Protection for Whistleblowers: Employees who raise concerns honestly and responsibly will not face any form of retaliation or discrimination.

    Consequences: Violations will result in disciplinary action, up to and including termination of employment.

    The basics we expect from everyone

    Be punctual and come to work in the required uniform

    Be honest with customers about price, product and delivery date.

    Follow the correct process when handling customer payments and documents.

    Keep customer information safe and confidential.

    Do not accept money, gifts or favours from financiers, insurers or vendors.

    Treat customers and colleagues with courtesy and respect

    Ensure all work and records are entered accurately in the system.

    Follow safety rules & procedures, including during test drives.

    • Every employee receives a copy of the Code of Conduct when they join the dealership and is expected to understand and follow its requirements.

    Types of Misconduct and Their Examples

    Misconduct is divided into two kinds:

    Minor misconduct

    Minor misconduct is usually a mistake, lapse in discipline. It is normally handled through a conversation with manager

    Examples
    Coming late repeatedly, or leaving early without permission
    Absent without informing anybody
    Not wearing uniform, or poor grooming
    Untidy work area, or not following the display standard
    Not attending training after being nominated
    Small arguments with colleagues

    Major misconduct

    It refers to serious actions that involves dishonesty, safety violations or behaviours that can harm people, the dealership environment, customers and JSW brand. Such cases are investigated through formal disciplinary process and may lead to termination of employment. please refer Section 10.2 for the same.

    Examples
    Theft or dishonesty with cash, stock, accessories or fuel
    Taking a customer’s payment into a personal account
    Taking money, commission or a gift from a financier, insurer, broker or vendor
    Booking a retail that has not happened or misrepresentation of any record
    Forging a signature or a document, including on a customer’s behalf
    Sharing or selling customer data
    Giving false information at the time of hiring, such as a qualification or a previous salary
    Sexual harassment (see 10.3)
    Abusive language, threats, or physical violence
    Coming to work under the influence of alcohol or drugs
    Driving a dealership or customer vehicle without a valid licence, or driving dangerously
    Deliberately damaging dealership or customer property
    Being absent without information for a long period
    Doing a job for another employer while employed here, dual employment
    Deliberately not following a lawful instruction from a manager
    Any act that breaks the law and impacting JSW images

    These lists are examples, not the complete list. Something not written here can still be misconduct.

    Employee salaries cannot be reduced as a punishment unless permitted by law. If the dealership needs to recover any loss, it must follow the proper legal process.

    10.2 The disciplinary process

    For minor misconduct

    StepWhat happens
    1The manager speaks to the person privately, on the day. Says what was wrong and what must change. Managers keep a record of the same.
    2If it happens again, HR issues a written warning. The person is expected to reply in writing.
    3If it continues, a final written warning is issued, and the person is given idea on next action.
    4If it continues after that, it is treated as major misconduct and goes through the full process below.

    For major misconduct

    StepWhat happensTime
    1The matter is reported to the HR Manager immediately. It can be reported by anyone in the organisation. Customers will reach to reporting manager of that person.N
    2HR makes a quick check of the basic factsN+2 days
    3A show cause notice is given to the person, in writing. It says exactly what they are accused of, with dates and details, and asks for their explanation.N+4 days
    4The person replies in writing. They must be given a fair chance to reply.N+6 days
    5If the reply is satisfactory, the matter is closed in writing. The person is told it is closed.N+8 days
    6If it is not satisfactory, or the facts are disputed, an enquiry is held. See below.N+15
    7Enquiry officer (as mentioned below) gives written findings to the Dealer Principal.N+18
    8The Dealer Principal decides the action and HR issue the order in writing, with reasons.N+20 days

    The enquiry

    If an employee does not attend the enquiry despite receiving proper notice, the enquiry may proceed in their absence. All notices issued and records of non-attendance should be documented and retained.

    Suspension during an enquiry

    • Used only where the person's presence would affect the enquiry, or where the matter is serious, such as theft or violence.
    • It is not a punishment. It is a pause while the facts are checked.
    • A subsistence allowance is paid during suspension, as the law requires.
    • If the person is cleared, they return to the same job and the balance salary is paid.

    Things to be careful about

    • Do not decide the outcome before completing the enquiry.
    • Maintain proper records of all documents, including notices, responses, investigation records, findings, and final decisions.
    • Do not discuss the matter around the dealership.
    • Do not let a manager handle a case where they are personally involved.
    • Apply the same standard to everybody regardless of the position or seniority.
    • If a criminal offence has taken place, such as theft, the dealership may also file a police complaint. The internal process still must be followed.

    Appeal

    If an employee believes a disciplinary decision is unfair, they may submit a written appeal to the HR Manager or Dealer Principal within seven days. The appeal will be reviewed, and a final decision will be shared in writing within fifteen days

    10.3 POSH: Prevention of sexual harassment

    This is governed by the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013.

    What counts as sexual harassment

    Any unwelcome behaviour of a sexual nature. This includes:

    • Physical contact or advances.
    • Asking for or demanding sexual favours.
    • Sexually coloured remarks, jokes or comments about a person's body.
    • Showing pornography.
    • Any other unwelcome physical, verbal or non-verbal conduct of a sexual nature, including messages, photographs and social media.

    The workplace includes the showroom, the workshop, the stockyard, the parking area, a customer's home during a visit, a test drive, an event, an outing and a work trip. It also covers work-related messages and calls outside office hours.

    The Internal Committee

    Every dealership with ten or more employees must have an Internal Committee also called as IC. This is a legal requirement, not a recommendation.

    PositionWho
    Presiding OfficerA senior woman employee of the dealership
    MembersAt least two employees committed to the cause of women, or with experience in social work or law
    External MemberOne member from an NGO or a person familiar with issues relating to sexual harassment. Not an employee of the dealership
    CompositionAt least half of the members must be women
    TermThree years

    Where the dealership has no senior woman employee, the Presiding Officer may be nominated from another outlet of the same dealer partner.

    How a complaint is handled

    StepWhat happensTime
    1The complaint is made in writing to the IC. If the woman cannot write it herself, the IC must help her put it in writing.Within 3 months of the incident, extendable by 3 months
    2The IC may first offer conciliation, if the woman asks for it. No money settlement is allowed as the basis of conciliation.Before the enquiry
    3The IC holds an enquiry. Both sides are heard. Confidentiality is maintained throughout.Completed within 90 days
    4The IC gives its report to the Dealer Principal.Within 10 days of completing the enquiry
    5The Dealer Principal acts on the recommendation.Within 60 days of the report
    6Either side may appeal.Within 90 days

    While the enquiry is going on

    • The person may ask for a transfer, for the other person to be transferred, or for leave of up to three months. This leave is in addition to her normal leave.
    • The identity of everybody involved is kept confidential. Discussing the case around the dealership is itself a disciplinary matter.
    • No action of any kind may be taken against the woman for having complained. Any pressure or unfair treatment after a complaint is major misconduct.

    What the dealership must do

    • Display the names and contact details of the IC members where everybody can see them.
    • Explain POSH to every new joiner during induction, including men.
    • Run an awareness session at least once a year through certified POSH trainer.
    • Train the IC members through certified POSH trainer.
    • File the annual return with the District Officer.
    • Include a POSH section in every appointment letter and the conduct code.

    A knowingly false complaint made to harm somebody is also a disciplinary matter.

    10.4 Grievance handling

    A grievance is any problem an employee has at work: pay, leave, a manager, workload, unfair treatment, facilities, or anything else.

    The steps

    LevelWhoTime to reply
    1Speak to the reporting manager.3 working days
    2If not settled, or if the problem is with the manager, go to the HR Manager in writing.7 working days
    3If still not settled, go to the Dealer Principal.15 working days
    4If the problem involves the Dealer Principal or the senior management of the dealership, the employee may write to JSW Motors directly.As per JSW Motors

    How to handle a grievance well

    • Listen fully before answering.
    • Write down what was raised and what was decided.
    • Give an answer even when the answer is no and explain why.
    • Keep it private.
    • Never punish somebody for raising a grievance in good faith.
    • Look for patterns. Several grievances from one team usually point at the team, not at the people complaining.

    Grievance committee

    If required by law, the dealership must establish a Grievance Committee with representatives from both employees and management. The committee should also include adequate representation of women. HR is responsible for monitoring legal requirements and ensuring the committee is formed in a timely manner.

    10.5 Best Practices

    • Be punctual, professional and customer focused at all times
    • Follow company processes and legal requirements without shortcuts
    • Report concerns or misconduct promptly and responsibly.
    • Treat customers, colleagues, and business partners with respect.
    • Protect the reputation of the dealership and the JSW brand through ethical conduct
    • Nobody is punished for raising a complaint or a grievance in good faith.

    Until now, we have covered the key HR policies, processes, and best practices for running a JSW dealership. These guidelines help create a professional, fair, and productive workplace.

    The next chapter explains how to apply these policies in day-to-day dealership operations.

    CHAPTER 11

    Organisation Policies

    11. Organisation Policies
    "Always treat your employees exactly as you want them to treat your best customers."
    OBJECTIVE:

    To bring together the dealership's day-to-day people policies in one place, so employees and managers have a single, consistent reference for how things are meant to work.

    CUSTOMER IMPACT:

    Consistent, well-understood policies mean customers receive the same standard of treatment regardless of which employee or outlet they interact with.

    11.1 Working hours and week off

    Working hours

    ItemRecommended
    Working hours9 hours a day including the break, and not more than 54 hours in a week
    Showroom timing9:30 am to 7:00 pm (or any other work shift assigned by the manager)
    Lunch break45 minutes
    Week offOne full day every week, on rotation. Usually a weekday for customer facing team members, because weekends are working days
    Working on the week offCompensatory off within 30 days, or overtime pay as per law
    OvertimePaid at twice the ordinary rate OR as the law requires. It must be recorded

    Roster

    • The manager makes the roster for the whole month and shares it via email before the month starts.
    • The manger also takes into account the shifts required to run the dealership operations.
    • Week offs rotate. The same person should not always get Monday while somebody else always gets a good day.
    • Showroom coverage comes first. The roster must always leave enough people on the floor on Saturday and Sunday.
    • If the weekly off is changed at short notice, the person is told the reason and given another day off that week.
    • During a festival period or a big campaign, week offs may be adjusted. Tell people in advance, not on the day.

    Women working at night

    Women may work after dark, but only if they agree to it and only if the dealership makes proper arrangements:

    • safe transport from the dealership to home
    • adequate lighting
    • security on the premises
    • never a woman working alone

    This is now also a legal requirement in many states.

    Late sitting

    • If people are kept back, arrange food and transport.
    • Late sitting should be the exception.

    11.2 Attendance

    Marking attendance

    • Use biometric system only.
    • Attendance is marked when arriving and when leaving.
    • Nobody marks attendance for somebody else.
    • For staff who go out for RTO work, bank work, home visits or deliveries, he/she should send a note to the reporting manager/HR, so they are not shown absent.

    Late coming

    SituationWhat happens
    Up to 15 minutes lateAllowed two days a month
    Late three times in a monthThe manager has a word
    Late more than three times in a monthHalf day leave deducted for each further late mark
    Habitually lateWritten warning from HR Manager

    If you cannot come to work

    • Inform the reporting manager before the shift starts.
    • Then apply for leave in the system on the same day or the next working day.
    • Absent without informing your manager is treated as leave without pay, and repeated cases are a disciplinary matter.
    • Absent for a period more than 5 working days without information is absconding which may lead to legal proceedings.

    Attendance records

    • Leave record must be updated.
    • HR closes attendance for the month by the date fixed for payroll, usually the 25th.
    • Any correction must be requested before the closing date. After payroll is processed, it is adjusted the subsequent month.
    • Records are kept as the law requires, and may be kept in electronic form.

    11.3 Leave Policy

    TypeHow many daysFor what
    Earned Leave12 days a yearPlanned leave, holidays, personal work. Applied for in advance
    Casual Leave5 days a yearShort, unplanned needs. Usually one or two days at a time
    Sick Leave5 days a yearIllness. Medical certificate needed if more than 2 days together
    Maternity Leave26 weeksFor the first two children. 12 weeks for the third onwards, as per law
    Paternity Leave7 daysRecommended, not required by law. To be taken within one month of the birth
    Bereavement Leave3 daysDeath of a close family member
    Marriage Leave3 daysOwn marriage. Once during service
    Compensatory OffAs earnedFor working on a week off or a holiday. To be used within 30 days
    Leave Without PayAs approvedWhen no other leave is left. Approved by the Dealer Principal

    New joiners earn leave after the probation period. Under the labor codes, the qualifying period for earned leave has come down, so HR should check the current position for its territory and state.

    Applying for leave

    Type of leaveHow much notice
    Earned leave, 1 to 3 daysAt least 3 days before
    Earned leave, more than 3 daysAt least 15 days before
    Casual leaveAt least 1 day before, or the same morning in an emergency
    Sick leaveInform the manager before the shift. Apply on return
    Maternity leaveAt least 8 weeks before

    Approving leave

    • The reporting manager approves. HR records it.
    • Answer within two working days.
    • Leave can be refused only for a genuine business reason, and the reason must be explained.
    • If leave is refused, offer another set of dates.
    • Not more than two people from a small team should be on leave at the same time, unless the manager agrees.
    • Before going on leave, the person hands over their work in progress jobs to a named colleague.

    Other leave FAQs

    QuestionAnswer
    Can earned leave be carried forward?Yes. Up to 24 days. Anything above is encashed or lapses as per the state rule
    Can leave be encashed?Earned leave only, at the time of leaving, and once a year if the dealership allows it
    Do casual and sick leave carry forward?No. They lapse at the end of the year
    Can casual leave be joined with earned leave?No. Casual leave is for short, unplanned needs
    Is a holiday inside a long leave counted?A holiday or week off falling in the middle of earned leave is counted as leave
    Leave during notice period?Only with the manager’s written agreement.
    Leave during probation?Casual and sick leave yes, in proportion. Earned leave is normally taken after confirmation

    11.4 Holidays

    • The dealership publishes its holiday list for the year before the year starts.
    • National holidays must be given: 26 January, 15 August and 2 October.
    • Other holidays are chosen based on the local festivals in that town.
    • Around 10 holidays in the year is normal.
    • A showroom may stay open on a festival day because customers want delivery on that day. Staff who work get compensatory off or holiday pay as per law.

    11.5 Travel Policy

    Most dealership travel is local: going to the RTO, the bank, a financier, a customer's home or office, or a nearby town for an event. Some staff also travel for training or meetings. The rules below cover both.

    Local travel

    How they travelWhat is paidRecommended
    Own two-wheelerPer kilometre₹ xx per km
    Own carPer kilometre₹ xx per km
    Auto, taxi, bus, metroActual fareReceipt where available
    Dealership vehicleFuel as per actualLog book entry needed
    • Local travel is claimed monthly, with the date, place and purpose written for each trip.
    • The claim goes to the reporting manager and is paid with the next month's salary.
    • Travel between home and the dealership is not claimable. That is normal commuting.

    Outstation travel

    Approved in advance by the Business Head, and by the Dealer Principal for Leadership roles.

    CategoryModeStayDaily recommended allowance
    JuniorBus, or train in sleeper or 3ACDealership guest house or a budget hotel₹ xxx a day
    MiddleTrain in 3AC or 2ACBudget hotel₹ xxx a day
    SeniorTrain in 2AC, or air where the distance and time justify itBusiness hotel₹ xxxx a day

    Daily allowance covers food and small expenses. If the dealership or JSW Motors is providing meals, the allowance is reduced accordingly. Amounts are recommendations only and to be confirmed based on local requirements.

    How to claim

    • Get written approval before travelling. An email or a signed travel form is enough.
    • Take a travel advance if needed. Ask HR at least two days before.
    • Keep the tickets and bills. A claim without a bill is settled only at the Business Head’s discretion.
    • Submit the claim within 7 days of coming back. Claims submitted after 30 days are not accepted.
    • The manager checks and approves, and Accounts settles it with the next salary.
    • Adjust any advance taken against the claim.

    Simple rules on travel

    • Travel by the cheapest sensible option.
    • Two people travelling to the same place should travel together and share a room where it is appropriate.
    • Claim only what was actually spent. A false claim is major misconduct under Chapter 10, however small the amount.
    • Personal travel added to a business trip is at the employee’s own cost.
    • Anybody driving on dealership work must hold a valid licence. Traffic fines from careless driving are the employee’s own liability.
    • Settle claims quickly.

    11.6 Best Practices

    • Working hours, week off and the holiday list are displayed at every outlet.
    • The roster for the month is published before the month begins.
    • Everybody marks their own attendance. Marking for somebody else is a disciplinary matter.
    • Leave is applied for in the system and approved in writing. Verbal permission is not leave.
    • A leave application is answered within two working days.
    • Working on a week off earns a compensatory off within 30 days, or overtime pay as per law.
    • Women working after dark do so only with consent and with safe transport arranged, and they should not be working alone.
    • Travel claims are submitted within 7 days and settled with the next salary.
    • Where the law in the state gives more than this chapter, the law applies.
    Women Working After Dark: Safety Checklist
    ✓
    Safe transport from the dealership to home
    ✓
    Adequate lighting
    ✓
    Security on the premises
    ✓
    Never a woman working alone
